# The tool creates whole files and owns whole files; it never edits Rust a human wrote

**ID**: `cpt-gearbox-adr-authoring-ownership-tiers`

## Table of Contents

<!-- generated by `cfs toc` -->

## Context and Problem Statement

PRD §4.2 currently forbids two things in one breath: *"Generating, modifying, or removing any
attribute macro in any gear crate"* and *"Migration tooling that drafts the declared half of a
`gear.gdl`"*. Both were written to protect the invariant in ADR
`cpt-gearbox-adr-macro-projected-catalogue`: every fact has exactly one author, and the Rust
attribute is that author for everything it can express.

Three usage scenarios have to be supported, and the second and third do not survive that ban.
Composing a product from existing gears is covered — `cpt-gearbox-usecase-switch-profile`. Creating a
**new** gear, in the platform repository or in someone else's, is not: it is absent from the PRD
entirely, while the actor it belongs to, `cpt-gearbox-actor-gear-author`, is defined in §2.1 and has
no use case at all. Creating a **plugin** is the same scenario with a host SDK dependency and a
`vendor` string. PRD §13 already holds the open question this raises: *"Which gear templates does an
integrator need, given that a template is the only place declared contract edges appear without
manual work?"*

So the question is not whether the tool may write Rust. It is **which files the tool owns**, which is
a question the generator design in `docs/plans/gearbox-builder-prototype.md` §7 already answers for
its own output and has never been asked about anything else. The current ban answers it by location
("nothing is ever written into `gears-rust`") rather than by ownership, and that is what makes it
block a new crate in a directory that does not exist yet.

## Decision Drivers

* The one-author invariant must survive intact. Whatever is permitted must not create a second place
  where a fact is written down by a human.
* A human must be able to see what will be written before it is written, and to undo it afterwards.
  This project has repeatedly found failures that were invisible rather than loud.
* Re-running must be safe. A scaffold that half-succeeded, or that duplicates its own output on a
  second run, is worse than one that refuses.
* The boundary must be stated as a rule a reviewer can apply, not as a list of forbidden verbs. The
  present §4.2 is a list, and it forbids by accident the single most common behaviour in comparable
  tools.
* Nothing here may require the platform repository to change. `gears-rust` is not ours.

## Considered Options

* **A — keep the flat ban.** Scenarios 2 and 3 become documented manual procedures: the tool shows a
  checklist, validates the result, and offers text to copy, as `GBX0208` already does.
* **B — ownership tiers.** Replace the ban with an explicit statement of which classes of file the
  tool owns, derived from what comparable tools permit themselves.
* **C — full permission.** The tool may create and also edit existing `#[toolkit::gear]` attributes —
  add a `dep`, add a `consumes` — from the UI.
* **D — three-way merge on the description.** The tool regenerates `gear.gdl` from source on every
  run and reconciles the human's edits, in the manner of Copier.

## Decision Outcome

**Chosen: B, ownership tiers.**

The survey in [More Information](#more-information) found a consistent six-tier convention across
Cargo, Kubebuilder, Angular, Rails, dotnet, Yeoman, Copier, Gazelle, Spring Initializr and Arduino
IDE itself. Stated as a rule:

> A tool may freely create new files, and may freely write files it declares itself the sole owner
> of. It may write into a file the human owns only at a location the human has explicitly
> designated, or in a form the human can trivially review and revert. It may never rewrite
> human-authored logic in place without version control to fall back on.

Mapped onto this project:

| Tier | Owner | Gearbox Builder |
|---|---|---|
| 0. New files | tool writes once, then hands over | **Permitted** — a new gear or plugin crate |
| 1. Tool metadata | tool, entirely | **Permitted** — `product.lock`, and it is marked read-only in the editor. Built: `ReadOnlyLockEditorProvider` rebinds Theia's `MonacoEditorProvider`, which is the only hook that can say "this file" rather than "this URI scheme". |
| 2. Generated source | tool, entirely, with a header | **Permitted** — the composition crates under `.gearbox/` |
| 3. Structured manifests | tool edits surgically | **Permitted** — one `members` entry in the workspace manifest, and one `use_gear(...)` entry in a `product.gdl` `gears` list ([amendment](#amendment-2026-08-29-a-gdl-description-is-a-structured-manifest)) |
| 4. Insertion markers in human files | tool owns a point, human owns the file | **Not needed** — see below |
| 5. Human logic | only under version control | **Forbidden**, unchanged |

Three findings decided this, and each narrows the change rather than widening it.

**No surveyed tool forbids tier 3.** Editing the manifest is the single most universal behaviour in
the set — `cargo add`, `dotnet package add`, Gazelle. The present §4.2 collapses tiers 3, 4 and 5
into one prohibition and so forbids the ordinary case in order to prevent the dangerous one.

**Tier 4 is not needed here, and that is a consequence of a decision already taken.** Angular
eliminated the need to edit `NgModule` by making components `--standalone`; Rails avoids editing
`config/application.rb` by dropping a file into `config/initializers/`. Both made the unit
self-describing so no second file needs surgery. Gearbox is already there: the catalogue finds a gear
by **walking the tree for `gear.gdl`** (stage S0 of ADR `cpt-gearbox-adr-staged-catalogue-loading`).
There is no registry to inject into. The only edit to an existing file in the whole scenario is one
line in `[workspace] members`, and that is tier 3.

**`GeneratedOnce` already means "scaffold".** §7 defines three ownership classes — `Generated`
overwrite, `GeneratedOnce` write-if-absent, `OperatorOwned` three-way merge — with `GBX0701`
(`crates/gearbox-ir/src/diagnostics.rs:576`) for an unresolvable conflict. A new gear consists
entirely of absent files, so `GeneratedOnce` covers it with no new vocabulary. This is why the
one-author invariant is untouched: the tool writes the attribute once, at creation, and never
returns to it. A fact written once by a machine and thereafter owned by a human has exactly one
author, which is the property ADR `cpt-gearbox-adr-macro-projected-catalogue` protects.

### Scope and boundary

This decision governs what Gearbox Builder may write, in any client — CLI, RPC, Studio. It does not
change what GDL may express, what the resolver decides, or where generated composition output goes.
It says nothing about the *content* of the templates; that is a separate question, and PRD §13's open
question about which templates an integrator needs remains open in that narrower form.

The boundary is drawn at **creation versus modification of an existing file**, not at file type. The
tool may write Rust into a crate directory that does not exist yet. It may not edit a `.rs` file that
does.

### Consequences

* **Scaffolding must be transactional.** All writes are staged and committed together or not at all,
  so a failed run never leaves a crate that is half-registered in the workspace. Every surveyed
  generator that edits more than one file does this; Angular and Yeoman both stage in memory.
* **Scaffolding must be idempotent by content.** The `members` entry is appended only if absent. This
  is Thor's rule and it costs nothing.
* **A preview is not optional.** Every surveyed tool has `--dry-run`; the plan's `FilePlan[]` with
  `create|update|unchanged|conflict` already provides the shape, so scaffolding reuses the generator's
  preview rather than inventing one.
* **`product.lock` becomes read-only in the editor.** Arduino IDE marks its own metadata read-only
  wholesale rather than protecting a region inside it, and that is the cheaper and clearer signal. A
  header comment asks; a read-only editor tells.
* **A second `Cargo.toml` write path appears.** `crates/gearbox-engine/src/manifest_check.rs` reads
  the manifest today to raise `GBX0209`; scaffolding writes what that check verifies. The two must
  agree, and the check is what proves they do — a scaffold that produced a wrong `lib` would be
  caught by the very diagnostic that exists for hand-written descriptions.
* **The tool acquires a failure mode it did not have: a half-written repository.** Mitigated by the
  first two consequences, and bounded by the fact that everything written is either new or one
  appended array element.
* **Nothing changes for existing gears.** The 14 described gears and the 30 undescribed ones in
  `gears-rust` are unaffected; `GBX0208` continues to describe rather than to act unless asked.

### Confirmation

* A scaffold into a directory that already exists must refuse, not overwrite — the `GeneratedOnce`
  contract, tested directly.
* Running the same scaffold twice must produce no second `members` entry and no diff.
* A scaffold interrupted between its first and last write must leave no trace, tested by injecting a
  failure at each write.
* The generated crate must pass `gearbox validate` with zero diagnostics, and in particular must not
  raise `GBX0209` — the check that already knows what a correct `crate_name`/`lib` pair looks like.
* No write may land outside the tiers. The writer takes an ownership class per file and refuses any
  path in a gear source root that already exists; that refusal is a test, not a review comment.

## Pros and Cons of the Options

### A — keep the flat ban

* Good, because it cannot possibly violate the one-author invariant.
* Good, because it is already written and needs no new machinery.
* Bad, because the scenario it blocks is the one every comparable tool supports, including the
  reference product: Arduino IDE's `File > New Sketch` is precisely tier 0.
* Bad, because the manual procedure it forces is where the mistakes are. `GBX0209` exists because a
  human deriving `lib` from a directory name gets `api_contracts` where Cargo produces
  `cf_api_contracts`. A template does not make that mistake.
* Bad, because `cpt-gearbox-actor-gear-author` remains an actor in the PRD with nothing to do.

### B — ownership tiers

* Good, because it states a rule rather than a list, so a case not yet imagined has an answer.
* Good, because tiers 0–2 are already how the generator works; only tier 3 is new, and it is the
  most conventional behaviour in the survey.
* Good, because it preserves the one-author invariant by construction, not by prohibition: writing
  once and never returning is single authorship.
* Bad, because it is more to hold in one's head than "never write". A reviewer must now classify a
  file before judging a write.
* Bad, because tier 3 is a genuine widening. One appended array element is small, but it is the
  first time the tool modifies a file it did not create.

### C — full permission

* Good, because it would enable genuinely useful edits — adding a `dep` from the graph view, adding
  a `consumes` from the contracts view.
* Bad, and decisively: it destroys the invariant. If a tool writes `#[toolkit::gear(deps = [...])]`,
  the attribute is no longer the human's single statement of the fact; it becomes a cache of a
  decision made elsewhere, and the question "who said this gear depends on cluster" stops having an
  answer.
* Bad, because both tools in the survey that rewrite human logic — `cargo fix` and `ng update` —
  gate it on a clean version-control tree, which is an admission that the operation is unsafe rather
  than a design for making it safe.

### D — three-way merge on the description

* Good, because it is the most capable mechanism found; Copier can reconstruct its own prior output
  and reconcile against it without storing a checksum.
* Bad, and decisively: it *assumes* that the tool's output and the human's edits legitimately occupy
  the same region, and it institutionalises that assumption by teaching users to resolve conflict
  markers. That is exactly the restatement ADR `cpt-gearbox-adr-macro-projected-catalogue` exists to
  prevent, arrived at by a different road.
* Bad, because `gear.gdl` declares only the disjoint remainder — the facts that *cannot* be derived.
  There is nothing in it for a merge to derive, so the machinery would carry no weight.

## More Information

### What comparable tools permit themselves

The convention below is drawn from published documentation and source, not from impressions.

**Cargo** draws the boundary at the manifest.
[`cargo new`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-new.html) writes a manifest, a sample
source file and a VCS ignore file; [`cargo init`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-init.html)
is explicit that "if there are typically-named Rust source files already in the directory, those will
be used" — it adopts existing source rather than rewriting it.
[`cargo add`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-add.html) "can add or modify
dependencies" and offers `--dry-run` ("Don't actually write the manifest"); it never mentions `.rs`.
The exception proves the rule:
[`cargo fix`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-fix.html) does rewrite source, and
carries `--allow-no-vcs`, `--allow-dirty` and `--allow-staged` — it refuses to run unless the change
is revertible.

**Kubebuilder** is the closest comparable, because it composes units into a runtime the way Gearbox
composes gears, and because it both scaffolds and injects.
[Scaffold markers](https://book.kubebuilder.io/reference/markers/scaffold) are comments of the form
`// +kubebuilder:scaffold:<type>` — `imports`, `scheme`, `builder`, `webhook` and six more — placed
in `cmd/main.go` and the test suites. The contract is stated plainly: *"If the marker is moved or
removed, the CLI will not be able to inject the necessary code, and the scaffolding process may fail
or behave unexpectedly."* The tool owns the point, the human owns the file. Kubebuilder also runs a
four-tier model: CLI-owned metadata (the `PROJECT` file), markers inside human files, human-owned
controller bodies, and fully generated files headed
`// Code generated by controller-gen. DO NOT EDIT.` — a form the Go toolchain
[standardises](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go) as the regexp `^// Code generated .* DO NOT EDIT\.$`.

**Angular** edits the user's `NgModule` when generating a component, and offers `--skip-import` to
decline and `--dry-run` to preview
([reference](https://angular.dev/cli/generate/component)). More interesting is where the framework
went: `--standalone` now defaults to `true`, so the generated component declares itself and no
second file needs editing. The framework changed so the tool would not have to do surgery.

**Rails** injects into `config/routes.rb` through
[`route`](https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/Rails/Generators/Actions.html), implemented over
Thor's `insert_into_file`, which is
[documented](https://github.com/rails/thor/blob/main/lib/thor/actions/inject_into_file.rb) as
reversible and refuses to insert content already present unless forced. Where it can, Rails avoids
the edit entirely: `initializer` drops a new file into `config/initializers/` instead of touching
`config/application.rb`.

**Gazelle** is the inverse model and the closest in spirit to this project. Build files are derived
from source; ownership is declared per attribute in a table inside the tool, and the
[merge algorithm](https://pigweed.googlesource.com/third_party/github/bazel-contrib/bazel-gazelle/+/HEAD/how-gazelle-works.md)
preserves any attribute that is not mergeable, which the documentation describes as "appropriate for
human-written attributes with a machine generated default". `# keep` is the per-instance override.

**Copier** stores its answers in `.copier-answers.yml` — a file it says
[must never be manually edited](https://copier.readthedocs.io/en/stable/updating/) — and on update
regenerates its own prior output, diffs to isolate the human's changes, and re-applies them, emitting
git-style conflict markers where they genuinely collide.

**Arduino IDE**, the reference product for Gearbox Studio, is the strictest of all and was read at
source. `File > New Sketch` writes a folder and one `.ino` from a hardcoded template
(`arduino-ide-extension/src/node/sketches-service-impl.ts`), overridable by the
`arduino.sketch.inoBlueprint` preference; nothing else is written, no manifest, no metadata. A search
of the repository for `scaffold` returns nothing, and `DO NOT EDIT` appears only in its own generated
protobuf stubs — **there are no insertion markers anywhere.** Exactly one command writes into a file
the human wrote: `Sketch > Include Library` prepends `#include` at `Range(1,1,1,1)` through Monaco,
bracketed by `pushStackElement()` on both sides so it collapses to one undo. It performs no
duplicate detection, which is tolerable only because it never returns to that insertion. And where a
file genuinely belongs to the tool — `sketch.json`, `thingProperties.h` — the IDE does not mark a
region inside it but makes **the whole file read-only in the editor**. Whole-file ownership, never a
region inside someone else's.

### Why the survey changes the answer rather than confirming it

The instinct behind §4.2 was that writing into a component's source is dangerous. The survey says
something more precise: writing into a file *someone else owns* is dangerous, and every mechanism in
the list — markers, headers, per-field schemas, content-match idempotence, staged commits, dry runs,
version-control gates — exists to answer the question "who owns this line". Gearbox has an unusually
good answer to that question already, and the tiers are that answer applied outward.

### When to revisit

* If `gears-rust` adopts glob `[workspace] members`, tier 3 becomes unnecessary and the tool stops
  modifying any existing file at all. That would be a strict improvement and this ADR should be
  narrowed.
* If the platform introduces a registry file that a gear must be listed in, tier 4 becomes necessary
  and Kubebuilder's marker contract is the model to copy — not Rails' inferred sentinels, because a
  marker is a fact the human authored once about where generated wiring goes, while a regex sentinel
  is a guess about the human's formatting.
* If a future feature needs to *change* an existing gear rather than create one, this ADR does not
  cover it and a new decision is required.

## Amendment 2026-08-29: a GDL description is a structured manifest

**Status: accepted. This extends tier 3; it reverses nothing.**

When this ADR was written, tier 3's only instance was `[workspace] members` in `Cargo.toml`, and the
question of whether a `product.gdl` could be edited was not asked. Studio's catalogue now wants a
toggle that puts a gear into the open product, so it has to be.

**A GDL description falls under tier 3, and tier 5 does not reach it.** Tier 5 forbids rewriting
*human logic*, and a GDL description cannot contain logic: `cpt-gearbox-fr-gdl-declarative` refuses
every branching construct in the dialect — `if`, `for`, `def`, `and`, `or`, comprehensions — and the
token scan raises `GBX0103` on each. What remains is declarations and literal data. A `use_gear(...)`
entry in a `gears` list is therefore a data entry in a list, in the same sense and to the same depth
as the dependency line `cargo add` writes. The tier-3 finding above applies unchanged: no surveyed
tool forbids this, and it is "the single most universal behaviour in the set".

The boundary in [Scope and boundary](#scope-and-boundary) — creation versus modification, not file
type — is what makes this an extension rather than a contradiction. That boundary was always about
ownership of lines, not about which language the file is written in. It said the tool may not edit a
`.rs` file a human wrote; it did not say the tool may edit only files it owns.

**Three limits come with it, and they are not negotiable separately.**

* **Only list membership.** The edit adds or removes one entry in a list literal. It does not
  reformat, reorder, normalise or evaluate. Editing `config = {…}`, profile bodies or bindings is
  outside this amendment and needs its own.
* **Span-surgical, never re-serialised.** The demo description is 105 lines of which 29 are comments,
  and the comments carry the reasoning for the decisions in it. A round trip through the interpreter
  would erase every one, which would breach the one-author invariant of ADR
  `cpt-gearbox-adr-macro-projected-catalogue` as surely as editing logic would: the author's
  explanation is part of what they authored. So the editor computes byte offsets from the AST and
  splices, and takes its indentation from the neighbouring entries. Where there is no span to edit —
  no `gears` argument, or a list produced by a helper rather than written literally — it refuses and
  says so, rather than guessing at a shape.
* **Refusal on an unsaved buffer.** If the description is open in the editor with unsaved changes,
  the write is refused. Writing would destroy an edit in progress, which is the failure this ADR
  exists to prevent, and worse than the one it worried about, because the tool would be the author of
  the loss. Saving on the author's behalf is not the alternative: that commits an edit they had not
  finished.

**`Ownership` does not apply, and is not stretched to.** The three classes in plan §7 —
`Generated`, `GeneratedOnce`, `OperatorOwned` — describe, by their own doc comment, who owns a
*generated* file. A `product.gdl` is an input, not an output. Forcing it into that vocabulary would
misrepresent both models, so a description edit carries no ownership class; what governs it is this
amendment and the refusals above.

The existing consequences carry over with one addition. Transactional still holds, by temp file and
rename in the same directory, so a crash cannot leave a truncated description. Idempotent by content
still holds: adding a gear the description already names is a no-op. "A preview is not optional"
still holds, and here it is met by `dry_run` on `product/addGear` and `product/removeGear` plus a
confirmation showing the exact line. The addition is that **a mutating RPC call is refused unless the
client declared `allow_writes` at initialize, and any path outside the declared workspace and source
roots is refused** — `cpt-gearbox-fr-rpc-writes-opt-in`, enforced in the engine rather than in the
client, because a client is not a security boundary.

### Confirmation of this amendment

* Adding a gear to the real `products/payments-demo/product.gdl` leaves all 29 comments in place and
  grows the file by exactly one line; removing it again reproduces the file byte for byte. Both in
  `cargo test -p gearbox-gdl`, and again through the interface in `npm run conformance`, where the
  assertion is that `git diff --stat` reports one insertion and no deletions. **The inverse being
  exact is the load-bearing test**: a re-serialising editor could pass the first half and could never
  pass the second.
* A `gears` list the editor cannot locate a span in produces a diagnostic, not a rewrite.
* A mutating call without `allow_writes`, and one with a path outside the roots, are both refused —
  ten such checks in `ide/scripts/rpc-smoke.mjs`.
* A dry run writes nothing: asserted by cancelling the confirmation and comparing against `HEAD`.

## Traceability

* Requirements: `cpt-gearbox-actor-gear-author` gains the use cases this decision unblocks;
  PRD §4.1/§4.2 carry the tier statement; PRD §13's template question narrows to content.
* Constrains: `docs/plans/gearbox-builder-prototype.md` §7 (the ownership classes this reuses).
* Depends on: ADR `cpt-gearbox-adr-macro-projected-catalogue` — the one-author invariant is what
  tiers 4 and 5 protect, and what `GeneratedOnce` leaves intact.
* Depends on: ADR `cpt-gearbox-adr-staged-catalogue-loading` — discovery by walking for `gear.gdl` is
  why there is no registry to inject into, which is why tier 4 is not needed.
* Amended by the 2026-08-29 amendment above: `cpt-gearbox-fr-gdl-declarative` is what places a GDL
  description in tier 3 rather than tier 5, and `cpt-gearbox-fr-rpc-writes-opt-in` is what gates the
  write. Implemented in `crates/gearbox-gdl/src/edit.rs`; the four client-side refusals are in
  `docs/plans/gearbox-builder-prototype.md` §9.2.

## Amendment 2026-09-01: any named argument in a literal list

**Status: accepted. This extends tier 3; it reverses nothing.**

The 2026-08-29 amendment limited tier-3 surgery to **list membership** in `gears`. Product authoring
now also changes **named arguments** inside calls that appear in literal lists on `product(...)`:

* `config = {...}` and `features = [...]` on a `use_gear(...)` entry;
* fields on `embedded(...)`, `host_workers(...)` and `kubernetes(...)` in `profiles = [...]`;
* `id` and `name` on `product(...)` when cloning.

The same three limits apply: span-surgical edits only; refuse when the list is not a literal; refuse
on an unsaved buffer. Scalar values only for `config` in this pass. Secret-like **config key names**
are refused by **heuristic** (see ADR `cpt-gearbox-adr-create-product`).

Creating a new `product.gdl` uses `writable_out_root` (path must not exist yet); editing an
existing description uses `writable_path`. Details: ADR `cpt-gearbox-adr-create-product`.

Implemented in `crates/gearbox-gdl/src/edit_call.rs` and the `gearbox/product/*` RPC methods added
in the same pass.

## Amendment 2026-09-02: Studio surface for tier 0 (New Gear)

**Status: accepted. This names the Studio surface for tier 0; it does not change the ownership
rule.**

Tier 0 remains what this ADR decided: the tool may create new files once and then hand them over.
Studio's surface for that is a **Gearbox: New Gear** command, a **FilePlan** preview before any
write (the same shape generation already uses), and writes that land under the declared **workspace**
and never inside a source root — the same boundary generation already enforces for
`writable_out_root`. Existing human-authored Rust stays untouchable (tier 5).

The **Gear** working context (ADR `cpt-gearbox-adr-domain-specific-ide-shell`) becomes reachable
only after this scaffold exists. Until then Home must not advertise New Gear or Open Gear.
